first.rationale: The two metrics actually degrading are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), and onboarding sits upstream of activation, so repairing the funnel entrance addresses both rather than one. Two independent inherited records converge here (memory_86 on shortened onboarding lifting completion and time-to-value, memory_31 on field reduction producing a durable first-week activation lift), which is why I spent both verification pulls on them: they are the load-bearing claims for the action I intend, and convergence between two archived records is worth confirming is not two consolidations of one original experiment. Promotional pricing is the tempting response to the competitor, but memory_73 explicitly records that it bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and warns against generalizing it; under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is a direct contraindication, not a tradeoff to rediscover. Referral incentives (memory_57) target established customers and do not touch the failing funnel; enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) is sound but addresses a segment that is not the source of the decline. Key caveats I am carrying forward rather than discarding: (1) both supporting memories are 15-64 days old and predate the competitor's entry, so the prior SMB population they were measured on may no longer be the population arriving today; (2) memory_31 measured activation, not retention or revenue quality, so a completion lift is not yet evidence of qualified revenue; (3) cutting signup fields has a real downstream cost -- those fields feed segmentation and the enterprise demo-request routing that memory_44 says outperforms self-serve, so stripping them could quietly degrade pipeline quality while the headline activation number improves. I will therefore instrument retention and enterprise-routing integrity as guardrails, not just completion rate, and will not read a completion lift alone as success. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout: the evidence is good but stale, and the downstream data-loss risk is not reversible after the fact.

final.rationale: Verification held and, importantly, confirmed the two records are genuinely independent rather than two consolidations of one experiment: exp_86 shortened the onboarding flow, exp_31 cut signup fields. Both are marked confirmed, so the convergence is real evidence. I am committing the slot to simplify_onboarding, weighted toward the exp_86 variant (compressing the flow itself) rather than the exp_31 variant (stripping signup fields), for three reasons. First, exp_86 targets the exact metric that is failing (completion +13%) and sits upstream of the activation decline, plausibly addressing both the -4% and the -6%. Second, exp_86 improved 30-day retention +3%, which is the right sign for a sustainable-qualified-revenue objective, whereas exp_31 showed retention -1%; exp_31's +4% qualified revenue is still a positive result, but it trades slightly against durability. Third, the field-cutting variant carries the downstream cost I flagged before verification and the archive did not resolve: signup fields feed segmentation and the enterprise demo-request routing that memory_44 shows outperforms self-serve on pipeline quality. Neither source record measured that, so choosing flow-compression over field-removal avoids an irreversible data loss the evidence does not cover. Promotional_pricing remains excluded despite being the direct answer to the competitor: memory_73 records that it bought acquisition at the cost of 30-day retention and explicitly warns against generalizing it. That is a contraindication under this objective, and competitive pressure is exactly the condition under which one is tempted to overwrite a warning that was written for this situation. Referral_incentive and enterprise_sales_assist are sound but do not touch the failing funnel or the declining segment. Residual uncertainty I am carrying, not discarding: both records predate the competitor's entry (day 52 and day 12 vs day 76), so the SMB population arriving now may be more price-motivated and less responsive than the one measured; exp_31 is explicitly SMB-only and not replicated elsewhere; and a completion lift alone is not evidence of qualified revenue. I will instrument 30-day retention, qualified revenue, and enterprise demo-request routing integrity as guardrails alongside completion, and will not treat a completion improvement by itself as success. Standard experiment rather than broad rollout: the evidence is confirmed but was gathered under a different competitive regime, and I would rather learn whether it still holds than assume it does.
